blocks.text: Stand anywhere on the edge of a circular field and look at the two ends of a fixed fence line across it. Wherever you stand on the same side, the angle you turn your head through is identical. That surprising fact is a circle theorem, and WAEC tests it every year.

blocks.markdown:
Circle theorems reward pattern recognition. Learn to look for four things in any circle diagram:

- the **centre** $O$, which means radii and therefore isosceles triangles
- a **diameter**, which means a right angle at the circumference
- a **cyclic quadrilateral**, all four vertices on the circle
- a **tangent**, which meets a radius at $90°$

rows: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc
The angle subtended by a diameter at the circumference is 90°
Angles subtended by the same arc in the same segment are equal
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment
The two tangents drawn from an external point are equal in length
blocks.caption: The seven theorems required by the WAEC and NECO syllabuses

blocks.title: Centre means isosceles
blocks.text: Every radius has the same length. So whenever a triangle has two sides that are radii, it is isosceles and its base angles are equal. This one observation solves a large share of circle questions.

blocks.caption: Angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc AB

blocks.title: Two tangents from an external point
blocks.prompt: Two tangents from an external point T touch a circle of centre O at A and B. If angle ATB = 50°, find angle AOB.

steps.text: A tangent meets a radius at 90°, so both angle OAT and angle OBT are right angles.
OATB is a quadrilateral, so its four angles add to 360°.
Subtract to find the angle at the centre.

blocks.markdown:
### Cyclic quadrilaterals

In a cyclic quadrilateral, **opposite** angles are supplementary. So if one angle is $85°$, the angle directly across from it is $95°$.

A second consequence follows: an exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the **interior opposite** angle. This is often the fastest route through a multi-step question.

items: Mark the centre, any diameters and any tangents on the diagram.
Mark all radii as equal, then look for isosceles triangles.
Identify which arc each angle stands on before comparing angles.
Quote the theorem by name for every step of your working.

blocks.title: Same arc, not just same look
blocks.text: The "angles in the same segment" theorem applies only when both angles stand on the **same arc**. Two angles that merely look similar in the diagram are not necessarily equal. Trace the arc with your finger before you claim they are equal.

blocks.title: Look for the diameter
blocks.text: If a chord passes through the centre, it is a diameter, and any angle it subtends at the circumference is exactly $90°$. Examiners often hide this by not drawing the centre clearly — check whether the chord passes through $O$.

points: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc.
The angle in a semicircle is 90°.
Angles in the same segment, standing on the same arc, are equal.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°.
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and tangents from an external point are equal.
Radii create isosceles triangles, which is often the key step.
